question.problem: Find the radius of the curvature for the curve $r(t)=⟨(1-t)^{2},\,{e}^{t}⟩$ at $t=0.$
question.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=(1-t)^{2},\,y(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-2(1-t),\, & {y}^{′}(t) & ={e}^{t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & ={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|-2(1-t)\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 2|}{({(-2(1-t))^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|2t{e}^{t}-4{e}^{t}|}{({(2(1-t))^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{|2(0){e}^{(0)}-4{e}^{(0)}|}{({(2(1-(0)))^{2}+({e}^{(0)})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{5}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
